notes: Care Standards Act de-registration JR; statutory construction and CST findings are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Moore: assured tenancies and continued registration as a care home
key_facts: Mental-health residents challenged the Care Standards Tribunal's refusal to cancel Alternative Futures' registration as a care home provider.
Alternative Housing granted assured tenancies while Alternative Futures continued to provide nursing and personal care at the same premises.
The Tribunal found coordinated day-to-day management and no material change in the level of care after the corporate restructure.
Residents argued assured tenancies meant the establishments ceased to be care homes within section 3.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a Care Standards Tribunal decision refusing cancellation of care home registration.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the Tribunal was bound to reject the appeal because accommodation with nursing or personal care still constituted a care home despite assured tenancies.
enrichment.ratio: An establishment remains a care home under section 3 of the Care Standards Act 2000 if it provides accommodation together with nursing or personal care, even where occupation is by assured tenancy and even if different companies provide accommodation and care; burden of proof plays no practical role on such appeals.
legal_issues: Whether assured weekly tenancies are incompatible with continued care home registration
Construction of 'establishment' and 'provides accommodation together with care' in section 3
Whether residents had sufficient interest to bring judicial review
Whether the Tribunal erred in emphasising lack of resident choice

notes: Joint NHS Part 36 offer appeals; costs and withdrawal principles are comprehensively analysed.

enrichment.short_title: Crouch and Murry: NHS settlement letters without Part 36 payments in
key_facts: Two NHS trusts sent standard 'offers to settle' in money claims without paying money into court under Part 36.3.
In Crouch the claimant beat the underlying merits threshold but recovered less than the offer; the judge ordered the trust to pay all costs.
In Murry the claimant belatedly sought to accept an earlier offer after rejecting it; Wright J treated Part 36 as applying by agreement and refused withdrawal.
The trusts sought Court of Appeal guidance that such letters should attract Part 36-style costs consequences.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Joined appeals on the costs effect of NHS settlement offer letters where no Part 36 payment in was made.
enrichment.outcome: Crouch appeal allowed: claimant ordered to pay trust costs from 21 days after the offer; Murry appeal dismissed and withdrawal discretion not disturbed.
enrichment.ratio: A defendant to a money claim cannot unilaterally obtain Part 36 consequences without a payment in, but under Part 36.1(2) and Part 44.3 a genuine NHS trust offer letter may be treated like a payment in when exercising costs discretion; withdrawal of an offer treated as a payment in requires a sufficient change of circumstances and funding changes are not generally sufficient.
legal_issues: Whether Part 36.3 requires a payment in for money-claim defendants
Admissibility and effect of Calderbank-style NHS offer letters
Whether parties can agree to treat an offer as a Part 36 payment
Exercise of discretion on permission to withdraw an offer under Part 36.6(5)

notes: Multi-offence sentence appeal; partial success on false passport possession only.

enrichment.short_title: R v Igbebion: bail conviction upheld and passport sentence reduced
key_facts: The appellant was convicted in 1999 of attempting to obtain services by deception at a bank and absconded until 2003.
While at large he possessed three altered passports and breached bail again before final sentencing in 2004.
He received a total of three years: 9 months for the deception attempt, 9 months consecutive for bail breach, 18 months consecutive for false instruments, plus 7 days for driving.
The judge had ruled that bail was clearly breached despite a speculative Magistrates' Court misunderstanding point.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal as of right on Bail Act conviction and application for leave to appeal against sentence, treated as substantive hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Bail conviction and most sentences upheld; 18-month consecutive sentence for possessing false passports quashed and replaced with 9 months consecutive.
enrichment.ratio: Failure formally to ask an accused whether he admits a Bail Act breach is an irregularity that does not vitiate conviction where guilt was clearly admitted through counsel's submissions; possession-only false passport offences on a guilty plea may warrant a lower consecutive term where totality is affected.
legal_issues: Whether conviction for breach of bail was invalid for want of a formal admission
Whether 9 months consecutive for bail breach was manifestly excessive
Appropriate sentence for attempted deception with no loss
Totality where multiple consecutive sentences were imposed after long absconding

notes: Pension top-up contract trial; declaration for claimant on natural reading of 1992 letter.

enrichment.short_title: Armitage v Staveley: early retirement letter and pension top-up increases
key_facts: Staveley reduced Mr Armitage's normal retirement age under the executive pension scheme from 60 to 58 by letter in July 1992.
The letter promised a pension calculated as if NRA were 58 and any excess over Inland Revenue limits would be paid by the company.
Inland Revenue caps limited scheme increases to 3% or RPI whereas SEPS rules entitled Category A members to 5% compound increases.
The parties disputed whether the company top-up included full 5% annual increases on the aggregate pension.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery trial of construction of contractual pension augmentation letters.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration for Mr Armitage that the 1992 letter entitles him to pension calculated ignoring Revenue limits, with Staveley paying any excess including 5% compound increases on the whole pension.
enrichment.ratio: On its natural reading a contractual letter reducing normal retirement age and promising to pay any pension that cannot be paid from the exempt approved scheme because of Inland Revenue limits covers both initial pension and subsequent 5% scheme increases, even though that exceeds Revenue caps and may appear generous with hindsight.
legal_issues: Construction of 'pension entitlement' and 'whole of the pension' in the employer letter
Whether Inland Revenue limits should be read back into top-up obligations
Implication of terms limiting top-up increases to Revenue-permitted levels
Interaction of Final Pensionable Salary and Final Remuneration under SEPS

notes: Attorney General reference on GP indecent assaults; increased extended sentence is fully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: AG Ref 79/2004: unduly lenient GP indecent assault and child image sentences
key_facts: A recently qualified GP indecently assaulted five female patients, including vulnerable elderly and young girls, often during bogus examinations.
Covert recordings of examinations were recovered from tissue-box cameras and his home computer.
About 1,600 indecent images of children were also found; he pleaded guilty to 23 of 26 counts.
He received an extended sentence of five and a half years with three and a half years custodial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the 1988 Act alleging unduly lenient extended sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; extended sentence increased to eight years with four and a half years custodial, reflecting double jeopardy on resentencing.
enrichment.ratio: Gross breach of trust by a doctor conducting unnecessary intimate examinations on vulnerable patients, with covert recording and large-scale indecent images, requires a substantially higher extended sentence than three and a half years' custody; good character and remorse afford only limited mitigation where standing in the community facilitated the offending.
legal_issues: Whether the Recorder's overall extended sentence was unduly lenient
Weight of breach of trust in medical examinations
Comparison with authorities on indecent assault and child pornography sentencing
Application of double jeopardy on Attorney General reference

notes: Joined homelessness review bias appeals; Ward LJ resolves conflicting county court decisions.

enrichment.short_title: Feld and Pour: apparent bias when same officer conducts second homelessness review
key_facts: Two homeless applicants challenged suitability decisions after final accommodation offers under Part VII of the Housing Act 1996.
In Feld, Ms Winborn conducted an earlier review and later reviewed the final offer of a one-bedroom flat for a chronically ill single man.
In Pour, Miss Obideyi conducted both the first and court-ordered fresh review of a studio flat offer to an elderly asylum seeker.
Conflicting county court decisions held respectively that there was and was not apparent bias.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Joined appeals to the Court of Appeal on points of law from county court appeals under section 204.
enrichment.outcome: Feld appeal dismissed; Pour appeal allowed and Judge Crawford Lindsay's quashing order set aside.
enrichment.ratio: The same housing review officer may conduct a second statutory review of a new final offer without apparent bias where no actual bias is alleged, the second review follows a fresh decision, and a fair-minded observer would expect a trained decision-maker to approach the task with an open mind despite earlier involvement.
legal_issues: Porter v Magill test for apparent bias in homelessness reviews
Whether regulation 2 prevents a second review by the same officer
Effect of Ombudsman involvement and internal discussions on impartiality
Whether Begum permits contracting out to avoid bias challenges

notes: Landmark diplomatic asylum/HRA challenge; comprehensive dismissal on jurisdiction and merits.

enrichment.short_title: R (B): diplomatic asylum claim for children in Australian immigration detention
key_facts: Two Afghan-origin brothers aged 12 and 13 sought refuge in the British Consulate in Melbourne after escaping Woomera detention.
They had suffered self-harm and exposure to tear gas and violence in long-term Australian immigration detention.
Consular officials sheltered them briefly but returned them to Australian authorities after London declined asylum intervention.
The applicants sought HRA declarations, mandatory orders and damages requiring future consular protection.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Permission to appeal against refusal of judicial review, converted into reserved full hearing on the merits.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; consular officials were not required to grant continuing diplomatic asylum or negotiate the children's release from Australian detention.
enrichment.ratio: Convention and HRA obligations can extend exceptionally to consular premises where fugitives are under UK authority, but diplomatic asylum is not generally required under international law or the Convention unless return would expose them to immediate serious injury; Australia as a rule-of-law state did not present the exceptional threat needed to justify refusing surrender.
legal_issues: Whether consular acts fell within UK jurisdiction under Article 1 ECHR
Territorial scope of the Human Rights Act 1998
Whether Soering/D positive obligations required continued consular refuge
Lawfulness of diplomatic asylum under public international law

enrichment.short_title: Goodway v Zurich: permission refused on Newbuild Tomlin order enforcement
key_facts: Zurich and builder Mr Goodway/Carabos settled consolidated proceedings over Newbuild latent-defect cover in a Tomlin order requiring remedial works and staged payment of £75,000.
Disputes over surveyor appointment and drainage defects delayed implementation of the settlement.
Zurich applied for mandatory enforcement of remedial works; the judge found mutual delay and no established breach justifying relief.
Mr Goodway sought to set aside the Tomlin order for misrepresentation about Zurich's £60,000 recovery from earlier Isle of Wight properties.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Single Lord Justice permission application with extension of time against Technology and Construction Court decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused on merits, retrial, and costs grounds; Tomlin order remained enforceable.
enrichment.ratio: Alleged factual inaccuracies and compendious rejection of misrepresentation claims do not show the kind of fundamental judicial inability to try the case fairly required for a retrial under Co-operative Group v ICL; mutual non-performance and alternative insurance cover can defeat mandatory enforcement of a Tomlin schedule without setting aside the settlement.
legal_issues: Whether the judge's findings contained material errors warranting retrial
Misrepresentation inducing entry into a Tomlin order
Mandatory relief for breach of Tomlin schedule obligations
Exercise of discretion on costs where both claim and counterclaim partly succeeded

notes: Section 36 reference for s18 wounding; sentence doubled with double-jeopardy adjustment.

enrichment.short_title: AG Ref 20/2004: unduly lenient sentence for steering-lock s18 wounding
key_facts: After a petrol-station queue dispute the offender and accomplices attacked an unarmed group with a knife and steering lock.
The offender repeatedly struck Mr Kanata over the head with the steering lock while an accomplice stabbed him.
Mr Kanata suffered catastrophic hypoxic brain injury and remains permanently tetraplegic and dependent on 24-hour care.
Following trial conviction on one section 18 count the offender received five years' imprisonment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 alleging unduly lenient sentence after trial.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; five-year sentence quashed and replaced with nine years' imprisonment after double-jeopardy reduction.
enrichment.ratio: A planned, unprovoked group attack with weapons causing permanent catastrophic brain injury warrants a post-trial section 18 sentence far above five years; good character and personal mitigation cannot adequately offset such gravity on an Attorney General reference.
legal_issues: Whether five years was unduly lenient for instigated section 18 wounding with permanent injury
Appropriate starting point after trial for weapon-led joint attack
Application of double jeopardy on reference
Weight of previous good character and psychiatric mitigation

notes: Child support capital allowances appeal; Court reluctantly allows absurdly low assessment construction.

enrichment.short_title: Smith v Smith: capital allowances in self-employed child support assessments
key_facts: Mr Smith, a self-employed car-fleet lessor to driving schools, appealed a child maintenance assessment based on his tax return.
Deducting capital allowances produced total taxable profits of about £20,892 and a weekly liability of £11.28 for three children.
Without deducting capital allowances the assessment would have been at the weekly maximum of about £318.
The case had generated 22 assessments since September 2001 without final resolution.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a Child Support Commissioner on construction of 'total taxable profits' in the 1999 regulations.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; capital allowances must be deducted under paragraph 2A and the matter remitted to the Appeal Tribunal, with departure directions available to the parent with care.
enrichment.ratio: Under the 1999 Child Support Regulations paragraph 2A, 'total taxable profits from self-employment as submitted to the Inland Revenue' means the figure in the tax return box for total taxable profits after deducting capital allowances; the anomaly with paragraph 3 does not justify reading capital allowances back in, though a departure direction may address lifestyle inconsistency.
legal_issues: Whether capital allowances are deductible in paragraph 2A child support calculations
Construction of 'total taxable profits' versus net profit plus depreciation
Relationship between paragraph 2A and the older paragraph 3 regime
Availability of departure directions for inconsistent lifestyle

Huxley v Child Support Officer [2000] 1 FLR 898
